# Differential item functioning and fairness {#dif}

<div class="goals">
**Learning goals.** After this chapter you can

* tell **impact** (a real difference between groups) from **DIF** (an item
  that works differently for people of the same ability);
* run an IRT likelihood-ratio DIF analysis and read its effect sizes;
* distinguish uniform from non-uniform DIF;
* run a Mantel-Haenszel DIF test and classify items with the ETS A/B/C rules;
* explain why anchor items matter.
</div>

**Key terms:**
[DIF](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#dif),
[reference and focal groups](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#reference-focal-group),
[uniform and non-uniform DIF](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#uniform-nonuniform-dif),
[DIF effect size](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#dif-effect-size),
[anchor items](https://www.okanbulut.com/mirtverse/articles/glossary.html#anchor-items).

## The ideas

Groups often differ in their average scores. That alone says nothing about
whether a test is fair: the groups may simply differ in what the test
measures, which is called **impact**. An item shows **differential item
functioning** (DIF) when people from different groups *with the same ability*
have different chances of answering it correctly [@holland1993]. DIF is a
statistical finding, not a verdict of bias; a content review decides whether
the reason is irrelevant to what the test should measure (bias) or a real
difference in what was taught.

We compare a **reference group** (often the majority group) with a **focal
group**. In IRT terms, DIF means the item has different parameters in the two
groups.

* **Uniform DIF:** the item is harder for one group at every ability level
  (the difficulty differs, the curves are parallel).
* **Non-uniform DIF:** the size or direction of the difference changes with
  ability (the slopes differ and the curves cross).

To compare groups we must first put them on a common scale, and that needs
items we trust to work the same way in both: the **anchors**. mirtverse's
`dif()` uses a *constrained-baseline* approach: it fits a multiple-group
model in which all item parameters are equal across groups while the group
means and variances are free, then frees each item's parameters in turn and
tests the change with a likelihood-ratio test. Items you do not test serve as
anchors. Because each test involves only one free item, the approach works
well when DIF is confined to a few items; when many items have DIF, a
*purification* step (testing, removing flagged items from the anchor set, and
testing again) is safer.

A significant test is not enough: with large samples tiny differences are
significant. `dif()` therefore reports effect sizes on the item score scale.
The signed version (`esd`) is the average difference in the probability of a
correct answer between the focal and the reference group at the same
ability; the unsigned version (`uesd`) also captures crossing curves.

The **Mantel-Haenszel** (MH) procedure [@holland1988] is the classical
alternative. It matches people on their sum score, builds a 2 × 2 table
(group × right/wrong) at every score level and tests whether the odds of a
correct answer differ between groups across the tables. ETS classifies the
size of MH DIF as A (negligible), B (moderate) or C (large).

## Example 1: paper versus tablet

A district moved its Grade 5 reading test from paper to tablets. We simulate
25 items answered by 1,200 students on paper (reference) and 800 on tablets
(focal). The tablet group is slightly weaker on average (impact). Two items
that ask students to drag text into a table are harder on tablets (uniform
DIF), and one long-passage item is easier for strong tablet readers and
harder for weak ones (non-uniform DIF).

```{r data-dif-1}
# Simulated 25-item reading test; `group` is the test mode for each student.
set.seed(909)
a <- matrix(rlnorm(25, 0.2, 0.25)); d <- matrix(rnorm(25, 0.2, 0.9))
a_tab <- a; d_tab <- d
d_tab[c(7, 18)] <- d[c(7, 18)] - 0.8          # R07, R18: uniform DIF
a_tab[22] <- a[22] * 1.8; d_tab[22] <- d[22]   # R22: non-uniform DIF
paper  <- simdata(a, d, N = 1200, itemtype = "2PL")
tablet <- simdata(a_tab, d_tab, N = 800, itemtype = "2PL",
                  Theta = matrix(rnorm(800, -0.2, 1)))
resp <- rbind(paper, tablet)
colnames(resp) <- sprintf("R%02d", 1:25)
group <- factor(rep(c("Paper", "Tablet"), c(1200, 800)),
                levels = c("Paper", "Tablet"))
```

The raw scores differ between the groups, but that alone does not tell us
which items, if any, are unfair:

```{r}
mode_resp <- resp; mode_group <- group   # kept for the exercises
tapply(rowSums(resp), group, mean)
```

`dif()` tests every item. Paper is the reference group because it is the
first level of the factor.

```{r}
res <- dif(resp, group = group)
res
```

The flagged items are the three we planted. The signed effect sizes of R07
and R18 are negative, meaning the items are harder for tablet users of the
same ability. R22's signed effect is small but its unsigned effect is
larger: the curves cross, so the advantages and disadvantages partly cancel
out on average.

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
gg_dif(res)
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.4}
gg_dif(res, type = "curves", which.items = c("R07", "R22"))
```

`interpret()` writes the findings up:

```{r}
interpret(res)
```

The baseline model also estimates the impact: the latent mean of the tablet
group relative to the paper group (fixed at 0).

```{r}
coef(res$baseline, simplify = TRUE)$Tablet$means
```

### Choosing anchors

If we already know some items are clean, we can test only the others: the
untested items become anchors. Here, as a check, we test only the three
flagged items against the other 22:

```{r}
dif(resp, group = group, items = c("R07", "R18", "R22"))$table
```

Does the DIF matter for scores? One way to judge is to compare the expected
total score of the test in the two groups at the same ability, which is
called differential test functioning. With two items that are harder for
tablet users and one that crosses, the total effect is a fraction of a score
point; a content review would still look at the drag-and-drop items, because
the problem can be fixed by changing the interface.

## Example 2: Mantel-Haenszel on a chemistry quiz

The MH test needs no IRT model, which makes it a good first screen and a
useful check. We simulate a 20-item chemistry quiz taken by 600 girls and
600 boys of equal average ability; item C11 involves a sports context and is
easier for boys of the same ability.

```{r data-dif-2}
# Simulated 20-item quiz; `group` is gender. C11 has uniform DIF.
set.seed(910)
a <- matrix(rlnorm(20, 0.2, 0.2)); d <- matrix(rnorm(20, 0, 0.8))
d_boys <- d; d_boys[11] <- d[11] + 0.7
resp <- rbind(simdata(a, d, N = 600, itemtype = "2PL"),
              simdata(a, d_boys, N = 600, itemtype = "2PL"))
colnames(resp) <- sprintf("C%02d", 1:20)
group <- factor(rep(c("Girl", "Boy"), each = 600), levels = c("Girl", "Boy"))
```

For each item we match on the total score of the *other* items, build the
stratified 2 × 2 tables and run the MH test. The common odds ratio
$\alpha_{MH}$ converts to the ETS delta scale as
$\text{MH D-DIF} = -2.35 \ln \alpha_{MH}$. The ETS rules call DIF negligible
(A) when $|\text{MH D-DIF}| < 1$ or the test is not significant, large (C)
when $|\text{MH D-DIF}| \ge 1.5$ and significant, and moderate (B) otherwise
(the full rules also test the size against 1).

```{r}
mh_item <- function(resp, group, item) {
  rest <- rowSums(resp[, colnames(resp) != item])
  strata <- cut(rest, unique(quantile(rest, 0:5 / 5)), include.lowest = TRUE)
  tab <- table(group, factor(resp[, item], levels = 1:0), strata)
  mh <- mantelhaen.test(tab, exact = FALSE)
  delta <- -2.35 * log(unname(mh$estimate))
  data.frame(item = item, alpha_MH = unname(mh$estimate),
             MH_D_DIF = delta, p.value = mh$p.value,
             ETS = ifelse(mh$p.value >= 0.05 | abs(delta) < 1, "A",
                          ifelse(abs(delta) >= 1.5, "C", "B")))
}
mh <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(resp), mh_item, resp = resp, group = group))
mh[order(mh$p.value), ][1:5, ]
```

The table is arranged so that $\alpha_{MH}$ is the odds of a correct answer
in the reference group (girls) divided by the odds in the focal group (boys),
at the same score. Values above 1, and negative MH D-DIF, mean the item
favours the reference group; values below 1, and positive MH D-DIF, favour
the focal group. C11 stands out, with a moderate (B) DIF in favour of boys. Matching on five score bands keeps the tables reasonably full
in a sample of this size; with more people you can match on every score.

The IRT analysis agrees:

```{r}
subset(dif(resp, group = group)$table, flag)
```

## Your turn

<div class="yourturn">
1. In Example 1, refit `dif()` with `p_adjust = "none"`. How many items are
   flagged now? Which result would you report, and why?
2. Run the MH procedure on the data of Example 1. Does it detect R22? Why is
   MH weaker for non-uniform DIF?
3. In Example 2, what happens to the MH results if you match on the total
   score *including* the studied item? On five versus ten score bands?
4. A newspaper writes that "the tablet test is biased because tablet users
   scored lower". Using the results of Example 1, write three sentences in
   reply.
</div>

<details><summary>Solutions</summary>

```{r}
sum(dif(mode_resp, group = mode_group, p_adjust = "none")$table$flag)
mh_mode <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(mode_resp), mh_item,
                                 resp = mode_resp, group = mode_group))
subset(mh_mode, item %in% c("R07", "R18", "R22"))
```

1. Without adjustment a few more items may be flagged at the 5% level by
   chance alone, since 25 tests are run. Report the adjusted results, and use
   the effect sizes to decide which items matter.
2. MH compares the *average* odds across score levels. When the curves cross,
   the advantage at one end and the disadvantage at the other cancel out, so
   MH (like the signed effect size) often misses non-uniform DIF. The IRT
   likelihood-ratio test, which frees the slope, catches it.
3. Including the studied item in the matching score is the textbook MH
   procedure; excluding it, as above, is a common variant. With 20 items the
   results are similar. More bands make the matching finer, but leave fewer
   people per table.
4. For example: "Tablet users did score a little lower on average, but most of
   that difference reflects a real difference in reading between the groups,
   not the test. When we compared students of the same reading ability, only
   three of 25 questions worked differently, and two of them involve dragging
   text on a screen, which we are redesigning."

</details>
